title: How Much Does Knowledge Matter For Teaching
author: Peter Greene
summary: Responding to a newspaper editorial that called subject knowledge the most important component of teaching, Greene sets out to rank what actually makes a teacher. He argues that content knowledge is indispensable, helping with classroom management, respect and adapting to teachable moments, using the image of a guide who knows the whole territory rather than only the paved path. But knowledge must be paired with the ability to explain, to read a room and to hold authority without tyranny. He rejects the slogans that diminish expertise, such as being just one more learner in the room. His conclusion places the desire to do the job first and subject knowledge second, since knowledge can be taught and care cannot, which undercuts warm-body substitute-teacher laws.
points: Subject knowledge supports everything else in a classroom, from management to responding to teachable moments.
A teacher needs to break knowledge into comprehensible pieces and read the room; expertise without communication fails students.
Greene pushes back on slogans like guide on the side when they are over-corrected into the teacher being just another learner.
He ranks wanting to do the job first and content knowledge second, because knowledge can be learned and care cannot be easily taught.
Lowering entry bars to recruit warm bodies does little, since the people who care about teaching are already in the profession.
quotes: I am a huge believer in the importance of subject matter knowledge. When you are standing in a classroom, there is no substitute for knowing what the hell you're talking about.

It's the difference between being a guide who knows the paved path to the destination, but is stumped if anyone takes one step off the asphalt, and a guide who knows every part of the territory, on the path and off, and can guide you to any spot from any other spot. I want a classroom with the latter.

But teaching also involves being able to convey that knowledge you have. Everyone knows (and some have experienced) the cliche of the person who's really smart but can't actually explain what they know to anyone else.
If you don't know more about what you're teaching than your students do, just go home. You are the grown up adult specialist. That is the gig.
I don't know how to teach you to give a shit about teaching, but I know lots of ways for you to learn the content so that you can do the job.
It's easy to find people with college degrees and warm bodies, but the people who want to teach and really care about the work are already there.
